Fourier rotation and directions at infinity

Written and self-checked by GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), Ultra, October 2026. Public domain (CC0).

The directions in which a Fourier support escapes to infinity bound every analytic singular direction. Homogeneity gives a stronger conclusion: Fourier transformation exchanges a nonzero base point and a nonzero covector, reversing the sign of the former. At a zero base point, physical support replaces the missing covector information. We prove these assertions for smooth wavefront and every admissible derivative-growth class, including distributions whose scaling law holds only away from the origin.

Our Fourier transform is , with inverse factor ; pairings are complex linear. We use the complete Schwartz Fourier foundation, F1–F5, and Tempered growth and spectral cutoffs, Lemma 2.1, for test seminorms, transpose identities and Schwartz convolution. Derivative growth and finite-order localization, Lemma 1 and Theorem 4, supplies fixed index shifts and controlled cutoffs. Cones and derivative-growth wavefronts, Lemmas 1–2 and Theorems 3–7, supplies their Fourier bounds, compact localization, comparison and differential rules; its flat-hypersurface calculation is used in an exercise. The smooth localization argument is also given in Boundary regularity and conic decomposition, Lemma 2, whose Theorem 3 proves the exact analytic boundary criterion.

The spherical representation, with all reciprocal-multiplier bounds, is Holomorphic decompositions of tempered distributions, Lemmas 1–2 and Theorem 3; the full polydisk Cauchy proof is Section 3 of Holomorphic boundaries in convex cones. The scaling and Euler equivalence and the resonant scaling law are Homogeneous extensions and angular moments, Lemma 1.1 and Theorem 4.1. Its angular foundation, A3, proves the finite point-jet theorem. The exact logarithmic transform is Radial powers and the logarithmic endpoint, Section 3, especially (3.2)–(3.7). Analytic composition is proved in Analytic maps and derivative growth, Theorem 3. Compactness, bumps and convergence use the supplied scalar foundation, Sections 12–13, and integration foundation, Sections 15–16. No external citation replaces any of these proofs.

The complete correspondence, including both origins

Theorem 5. Suppose is homogeneous of some complex degree on . For every admissible ,

All three equivalences also hold for ordinary smooth wavefront. In particular they hold at the analytic endpoint. The support assertions concern the complete distributions, including their point terms.

Proof: nonzero base and covector. Lemma 2 writes , with globally homogeneous. Both corrections in physical space and frequency space are analytic off zero, hence belong to every there. Applying the finite-sum inclusion in both directions shows that adding them leaves wavefront unchanged on those open sets. This also holds for smooth wavefront by the fixed-cutoff definition. Apply Lemma 3 to to obtain the first line of (24).

Proof: physical support and the Fourier origin. Punctured homogeneity makes the punctured support invariant under every positive dilation: the distributional change of variables carries a zero open set to its dilation, and the scalar is nonzero. If is outside support, a small ball about it and all its positive dilations are zero sets. Their union contains a conic neighborhood of its ray. Consequently the direction of is absent from the limit cone of . The double Fourier transform is ; Theorem 1 applied to therefore excludes even from analytic wavefront. It excludes it from all the other classes as well.

Conversely suppose is absent from ordinary . By definition there is a compact smooth near zero such that is rapidly decreasing in a conic neighborhood of . Choose a small closed ball about , avoiding zero, whose negative directions lie in that cone. On this ball the left side of (20) tends uniformly to zero; the fixed factor is absorbed by taking a larger decay power. The remainder tends uniformly to zero too. Thus tends to zero as a distribution on the ball's interior. Lemma 4 also makes it converge there to . Uniqueness of distributional limits gives on that neighborhood. Hence is outside support. We have proved the support equivalence with ordinary wavefront; the analytic exclusion in the first direction and the comparisons prove the middle line for every .

Proof: Fourier support and the physical origin. If globally, then is globally homogeneous. Apply the middle equivalence to , and use the double transform and reflection. This proves the last line.

If , it is a nonzero finite point jet. Its Fourier transform is a nonzero polynomial. Such a polynomial cannot decrease rapidly on any open cone: its highest nonzero homogeneous part cannot vanish on an open set, since the exact finite Taylor expansion would then make that polynomial identically zero. Choose a direction in the cone where that part is nonzero; along its ray the top power dominates the lower powers. Every cutoff equal to one near zero leaves unchanged, so .

Differential operators with smooth coefficients do not enlarge ordinary wavefront. Here is the needed local argument. If has rapid transform in a cone and near the base point, take on a smaller neighborhood with support where . For , . Fourier differentiation preserves rapid decay, and multiplication by the compact smooth preserves it on a smaller cone by the earlier convolution estimate. This proves the assertion. Apply it to . Thus has every nonzero smooth wavefront direction at zero, and comparison gives every direction there.

The nonzero polynomial on the right cannot do so. Hence . Both sides of the last equivalence in (24) now hold for every nonzero . This proves the nonhomogeneous case and finishes the theorem.

Exercises with complete solutions

Exercise 1 — bounded spectral translation (foundation). Prove that for every fixed vector . Apply this to modulation of a tempered distribution. What does Theorem 1 say for compact Fourier support?

Solution. If and , then ; apply the same argument with for the reverse inclusion. Direct Fourier substitution shows that multiplying by translates its Fourier support by . Thus the bound (2) is unchanged. In fact every wavefront class itself is unchanged: multiplication by that analytic function cannot enlarge , and multiplication by its analytic inverse proves the reverse inclusion. The fixed-cutoff convolution rule gives the smooth assertion. If Fourier support is compact, (1) is empty and Theorem 1 says is analytic everywhere by the analytic projection theorem. For an entire extension of itself, choose a compact smooth near its Fourier support and use . On the fixed compact frequency support, every parameter Taylor remainder tends to zero in the finite test seminorms controlling the pairing. The Cauchy–Riemann equations and polydisk argument prove holomorphy for every , and Fourier inversion identifies its real trace with .

Exercise 2 — a nonempty limit cone with no singularity (intermediate). In , define the finite measure

Determine its spectral limit cone and prove that is analytic on all real space. Explain what this says about equality in (2).

Solution. The total mass is one, so is tempered by the supremum seminorm. Its support is exactly the displayed discrete closed set: each point has positive mass and a small isolating ball; every bounded set meets only finitely many points. Its normalized direction is . Every escaping sequence has indices tending to infinity, so .

Fourier inversion as a distribution gives ; the absolute uniform convergence also identifies it as an ordinary continuous function. On a compact complex set with and , the absolute terms are bounded by . For , the square inequality gives . The resulting geometric series converges uniformly. On slightly larger compact sets in the same tube, the polydisk Cauchy formula justifies differentiation of the convergent sum and proves holomorphy. Every real point lies in that tube, hence . The upper bound (2) can therefore be strict even with an unbounded, nonempty Fourier support.

Exercise 4 — a point term changes the origin (foundation). On , let . Give its Euler defect for the punctured degree , its Fourier transform, and both wavefront sets in (24).

Solution. The point-jet identity gives , although is degree-zero homogeneous away from zero. Fourier inversion gives . Both distributions have full physical support, are analytic off zero, and have every nonzero smooth direction at zero because their nonzero point terms have polynomial Fourier transforms and adding an analytic function does not change wavefront. Thus both all- wavefronts equal . The first line of (24) is empty on both sides, while both origin formulas are nonempty. Dropping point terms would lose precisely this information.

Exercise 6 — a resonant second derivative (advanced). For every , take . Determine its punctured degree, Euler defect, Fourier transform and both physical supports. Determine its smooth and all- wavefronts and those of its transform.

Solution. The degree off zero is . The commutator used in Lemma 2 and (8) give , and . The latter expression denotes the full regular logarithm multiplied by a polynomial; no unspecified point term is being discarded. It is analytic off zero. The nonzero Euler defect and (25) show its support is the whole space, even though its function can vanish on a hyperplane.

Off zero, direct differentiation gives . Its numerator is a nonzero polynomial in every positive dimension, hence cannot vanish on any nonempty open set. Every open ball avoiding zero therefore contains a region where this analytic function is nonzero, and every neighborhood of zero contains such a ball. Thus too. Both distributions are analytic off zero. The two origin equivalences now give exactly for both smooth wavefronts and every -wavefront. A zero along an isolated ray or hypersurface is not a zero on an open frequency cone.
